title: Building the craft of Cold Call
author: Bronwyn Ryrie Jones
summary: Bronwyn Ryrie Jones argues that Cold Call is a multi-faceted instructional craft and not merely the act of calling on a non-volunteer. She defines it as the teacher inviting a student to respond without waiting for a volunteer, with selection driven by teacher judgment rather than chance. She codifies four steps: pose and repeat the question, have all students rehearse a response, scan responses with purpose, and then select students warmly. The piece makes a pointed case against randomising tools such as tins of name sticks, which bypass the monitoring, noticing and differentiating that expert teachers do. She considers and rejects the view that sticks scaffold novice confidence, arguing they make teachers more wedded to the lottery. She closes with a three-priority route to building real expertise and staffroom reflection questions.
points: Cold Call's visible moment, selecting a student, takes a split second, but it sits on top of a bundle of moves including all-student rehearsal, purposeful roving and judgment about which response to surface.
Randomised selection removes the incentive to listen to the room, so the skills that make Cold Call valuable may never develop.
Teachers can differentiate a Cold Call through tone, question difficulty or a repeated sentence frame, but only if they choose the student deliberately.
Schools should first unlearn default volunteer-driven participation, then secure every student's participation, and only then layer in intentional cold calling.
The staffroom prompts turn the argument into PD: what information drives selection, what all-student routines exist, and how roving is done.
quotes: Rushing implementation of Cold Call is a mistake because it’s a multi-faceted craft that takes time to hone. The most visible bit — selecting a student — takes a split-second.
I define Cold Call like this: Without waiting for a volunteer, the teacher invites a student to respond to a specific question or prompt.

If you randomise Cold Calling, it’s entirely possible that you skip the development of these skills altogether. If you rely on rattling a tin and pulling a student’s name on a stick, what is the point in listening intently to capture ideas around the room?
The selection mechanism itself is doing almost none of the meaningful instructional work.
The sticks solve the problem of choosing a student to ask, and in turn provide no incentive for teachers to get better at judging this themselves.
Equity and excellence, in all aspects of teaching, cannot be achieved by lottery.

Priority 2: Support your teachers to become practised at the hardest thing of all – securing every student’s participation. Develop school- or faculty-wide techniques for this to happen regularly in every single lesson.
